headline: Huang's Nvidia return sparks huge stock rally
summary: Stocks jumped on Monday after Nvidia brought Jensen Huang back as CEO following pressure from Trump, which restored faith in the [[AI trade]] after the [[S&P 500]] had fallen four straight weeks. The S&P 500 rose 4.73% to 7237.17 and the [[Nasdaq]] gained 6.51%, which is a huge move for a single day and was the best day for US stocks in more than a year. Because investors suddenly felt safer, the [[VIX]] (a gauge of how much fear is in the market) dropped 25.83% to 26.62, though that is still a fairly nervous level. Oil fell 4.29% to 80.38 as crude kept flowing out of the Persian Gulf, while the dollar rose 0.49% on bets that the Fed will keep leaning hawkish. Gold also jumped 3.44%, and it's not obvious why, since a calm stock rally and a stronger dollar usually weigh on it.
one_thing: One personnel decision at Nvidia moved the whole market, which shows how much of the S&P 500 now rides on a few AI names. The catch is that Congress and a reported SEC probe mean the relief could be fragile.

cross_asset.stocks: The S&P 500 rose 4.73% to 7237.17, the Dow rose 3.01% to 49595.31 and the Nasdaq rose 6.51% to 24089.56. The Nasdaq won because it is packed with AI-linked tech, so the Nvidia news hit it hardest, and Oracle and CoreWeave also jumped on the bet that Nvidia's financing of the AI ecosystem keeps flowing. Safer corners like Kroger and Tyson Foods lagged, which tells you money left the hiding places and went back into growth.
cross_asset.rates: The [[10-year yield]] rose 1 [[basis point]] to 4.92%, which is a tiny move. Last week yields fell because worried investors bought safe [[Treasuries]], so when stocks recovered that safe-haven bid faded, which is why yields didn't fall further. The 2-year yield sits at 4.63%, well above the Fed's 3.875% rate, which means the market already prices in some rate hikes, and the gap between the 10-year and 2-year is +29 basis points.
cross_asset.fx: The [[dollar index]] rose 0.49% to 104.32, with headlines crediting hawkish Fed bets and not the election. Sterling and the euro edged up in the morning as the stock rebound trimmed the dollar's appeal, but by the close the dollar was higher again. USD/JPY slipped 0.49% to 158.93, so the yen strengthened a bit, and the reason isn't clear since the dollar was broadly stronger.
cross_asset.commodities: WTI crude fell 4.29% to 80.38, its lowest settle since August, because oil kept flowing out of the Persian Gulf even though attacks on tankers continue. Cheaper oil is good news for gas prices and for inflation worries. Gold rose 3.44% to 3636.3 even as stocks soared, and the cause of that jump isn't obvious from today's headlines.

storylines.name: AI trade jitters
storylines.backstory: Markets leaned on the biggest AI-linked tech firms, so doubts about AI hit the whole index. Nvidia's CEO left on Nov 12, a selloff followed, official papers warned that AI [[valuation]]s look stretched, and the S&P 500 fell four straight weeks.
storylines.today: Nvidia's board approved Huang's return and Reuters says Trump pressured the company to do it. The Nasdaq rose 6.51% and the S&P 500 had its best day in more than a year, with Oracle and CoreWeave also jumping on the bet that Nvidia's money keeps flowing through the AI ecosystem. The cheering came with pushback, because lawmakers of both parties questioned Trump's view that Huang is not a national security risk, Treasury Secretary Bessent reversed his harder line on Nvidia, staff abuse allegations surfaced and a reported SEC probe is in the news. A strategist also warned that Wall Street is not pricing in a [[data center]] slowdown, and HPE posted its strongest growth ever but its stock wavered.
storylines.market_link: A handful of AI giants make up a big slice of the S&P 500, so when Nvidia's leadership looked shaky the whole index fell, and when Huang came back the whole index bounced. That swing changes how nervous investors are, which is why the [[VIX]] dropped 25.83%. When fear falls, money leaves defensive stocks like Kroger and Tyson and goes back into growth, and safe-haven buying of Treasuries cools, which keeps yields from falling.
storylines.next_chapter: Watch whether Congress or the reported SEC probe turns into real action against Nvidia, and whether other AI firms back up the good news with results, because HPE showed that strong AI numbers don't lift every stock.
note: Nvidia is so big that one CEO decision moves the whole index.
Interview line: the rally shows AI sentiment is concentrated, so index risk is really single-name risk.

storylines.name: Central banks vs energy inflation
storylines.backstory: The Iran war cut oil supply and pushed up headline inflation, so central banks must decide whether the price jump fades or leaks into wages and services. Euro area inflation hit 4%, the Bank of England hiked to 4% and the Fed sits at 3.875%.
storylines.today: Fed's John Williams said higher interest rates are likely 'over time' to address inflation, but he is confident inflation gets closer to 2% in 2027. Waller said the Fed meets Dec 8 and 9, and Cook said damaged infrastructure and low inventories could keep oil prices high for a long time. Japan's core inflation hit its highest this year as an energy subsidy ended.
storylines.market_link: If officials signal higher rates, investors expect borrowing to get pricier, so the 2-year yield (which tracks the Fed closely) rises first, now at 4.63% against a Fed rate of 3.875%. Higher US rates also make dollars more attractive to hold, which helps the dollar. A San Francisco Fed paper adds a wrinkle: when inflation comes from supply problems like oil, Fed surprises pass less strongly into longer-term yields, so the 10-year may move less than the 2-year.
storylines.next_chapter: The Fed meeting on Dec 8 and 9 is the next big test, and oil prices will shape how hawkish officials sound before then.
note: 2-year 4.63% vs Fed rate 3.875% means hikes are partly priced.
Williams: higher rates 'over time', inflation nearer 2% in 2027.
Interview line: supply-driven inflation is harder for the Fed to fight because rate hikes can't make more oil.

storylines.name: Iran war and oil
storylines.backstory: The conflict began in early 2026 and cut global oil output by 12 mb/d in March, but prices stayed below records because stored oil filled the gap. The IEA says the Hormuz shock lifted the world's oil and gas import bill 25% to $1.6 trillion.
storylines.today: WTI fell 4.29% to 80.38, its lowest settle since August, because oil kept flowing out of the Persian Gulf even though tanker attacks continue. A headline says China has become the top oil buyer, and Trump suggested recent gas price drops are tied to the election, calling it 'a giant hoax' in one headline.
storylines.market_link: Oil got cheaper, which means gasoline and shipping costs should ease, so inflation worries can cool and central banks feel less pressure to hike. Cheaper oil is also a cost break for airlines and factories, which supports stocks. The catch is that Cook warned damaged infrastructure and low inventories could keep prices high for a long time, so the relief may not last.
storylines.next_chapter: Watch whether tanker attacks start to block flows out of the Gulf, because that would flip the story back to supply fear.
note: WTI -4.29% to 80.38, lowest settle since August.
Oil flowing + cheaper oil = lower inflation pressure.
Interview line: oil is a tax on consumers, so a falling price works like a tax cut.

storylines.name: US midterms and the dollar
storylines.backstory: The midterms produced what headlines call a Democratic rout, and markets asked how divided government might change tariffs, spending and the dollar. The dollar then had its biggest rally since 2024.
storylines.today: The dollar index rose 0.49% to 104.32 and headlines credit hawkish Fed bets, not the election. Goldman Sachs expects the rally to continue in the coming months and fade in 2027, though its technical read says the dollar is [[overbought]] and could slow. Sterling and the euro edged up in the morning, but the dollar was higher again by the close.
storylines.market_link: If traders think the Fed will keep rates higher than other central banks, investors want dollars to earn that extra yield, so the dollar rises. A stronger dollar makes imports cheaper for Americans but makes dollar debts and US exports harder for the rest of the world. A dollar that is overbought can pause or reverse quickly if rate bets cool.
storylines.next_chapter: Fed speakers and the Dec 8 and 9 meeting will decide whether the hawkish bet holds, and the US GDP and personal income data ahead of Thanksgiving may nudge it.
note: Dollar index +0.49% to 104.32.
Cause is Fed rate bets, not the election.
Interview line: currencies follow interest rate gaps, and the Fed gap is the dollar's engine.

stories.title: Huang's return restores the AI rally
stories.what: Nvidia's board approved Jensen Huang's return as CEO and stocks soared, with the S&P 500 up 4.73% and the Nasdaq up 6.51%. Oracle and CoreWeave also jumped.
stories.why: Nvidia spends and lends heavily across the AI ecosystem, so investors read its stability as a sign the AI money keeps flowing. In other words, the market is trading on confidence in one company, which shows how concentrated the index has become.
stories.watch: Whether the rally survives scrutiny from Congress and the reported SEC probe.

stories.title: Washington pushes back on Nvidia's decision
stories.what: Lawmakers of both parties questioned Trump's conclusion that Huang is not a national security risk. Bessent reversed his harder line, and a reported SEC probe and staff allegations surfaced.
stories.why: A company that is this central to the market can't easily shake political risk, so any real action against Nvidia could hit the whole AI trade and not just one stock.
stories.watch: Any formal hearing, regulator step or new restrictions tied to Nvidia.

stories.title: Oil slides to its lowest since August
stories.what: WTI fell 4.29% to 80.38 as crude kept flowing out of the Persian Gulf despite attacks on shipping.
stories.why: Cheaper oil means lower gas prices, which helps households and eases inflation worries, so central banks may feel less pressure to hike. The risk is that Cook says infrastructure damage and low inventories could keep prices high for a long time.
stories.watch: Tanker attacks and whether Gulf flows stay steady.

stories.title: Williams signals higher rates over time
stories.what: Fed's John Williams said higher rates are likely 'over time' to address inflation while expressing confidence inflation nears 2% in 2027. The 2-year yield is 4.63% against the Fed's 3.875%.
stories.why: A hawkish Fed keeps short-term yields high and supports the dollar, which tightens financial conditions for borrowers worldwide.
stories.watch: The Fed meeting on Dec 8 and 9 and any more speeches before it.

stories.title: Safe stocks lag as money chases growth
stories.what: Consumer stocks such as Kroger and Tyson Foods were among the S&P 500's biggest losers while Nvidia stormed higher.
stories.why: These stocks had been a hiding place amid cracks in the AI trade, so their drop shows investors rushing back into riskier assets and shows how quickly the mood flipped.
stories.watch: If the AI rally stalls, safe stocks could attract money again.

under_the_radar.title: Lagarde's last Frankfurt banking speech
under_the_radar.what: ECB President Christine Lagarde said her speech at the Frankfurt European Banking Congress would be her last there. Her message was about acting early, because by the time a problem is obvious the best time to act has usually passed. She also stressed Europe's exposure to dependencies like critical raw materials and technology.
under_the_radar.chain: Euro area inflation is 4% while the ECB's rate is 2.5%, so a message about acting early could hint at pressure to tighten policy. If markets start expecting ECB hikes, euro area yields would rise, the euro could strengthen against the dollar and European stocks could feel the pinch from higher borrowing costs. Nothing in today's headlines says the ECB is about to move, so this is a theme and not a signal.
under_the_radar.watch: Any ECB speaker who links high inflation to a rate hike, or news on who leads the ECB next.
note: Euro area inflation 4% vs ECB rate 2.5%.
Lagarde's theme: act early before the problem is obvious.
Interview line: the ECB's rate sits well below inflation, so the next move is the debate.

under_the_radar.title: ECB widens collateral to tokenised assets
under_the_radar.what: The ECB will accept assets issued on approved [[DLT]] platforms as collateral for its credit operations. Details arrive in spring 2027 and implementation is planned for June 2027.
under_the_radar.chain: Collateral is what banks hand over to borrow from the central bank, so accepting tokenised assets makes them more useful and more attractive to issue. Over time that could grow the market for tokenised bonds and make settlement faster, which matters for banks and for the plumbing of European funding markets. The effect on prices today is tiny.
under_the_radar.watch: The detailed requirements the Eurosystem plans to publish in spring 2027.
note: Implementation planned for June 2027.
Collateral eligibility is the funding plumbing banks depend on.
Interview line: the ECB is opening its collateral rules to tokenised assets, carefully and slowly.

under_the_radar.title: US labor supply may start to shrink
under_the_radar.what: A New York Fed post says growth in the US working-age population has fallen to near zero after a sharp drop in net immigration, so the available labor supply could soon begin to shrink.
under_the_radar.chain: Fewer available workers means companies may compete harder on pay, which can lift wages and keep service prices sticky. That would make the Fed's job harder at a time when oil already pushes inflation up, so it could support the case for higher rates and a firmer dollar. It also hints at slower long-run growth.
under_the_radar.watch: Wage data and any Fed speaker linking labor supply to inflation.
note: Working-age population growth near zero.
Less labor supply can mean stickier wages and inflation.
Interview line: shrinking labor supply is an inflation risk the Fed can't fix with rates.

deep_dive.why_now: The AI trade just swung wildly on one CEO headline, so knowing how the big AI firms pay for their buildout tells you how fragile or solid the story really is.
key_points: The St. Louis Fed looks at 10 large tech firms, which it calls hyperscalers, including Alphabet, Amazon, Microsoft, Nvidia and Oracle.
Their high profits let them fund much of their investment with their own money.
Their debt compared with assets fell from nearly 30% in 2023 to roughly 25% in early 2026, while other public US firms stayed near 34%.
Their payouts to shareholders dropped from about 4% of assets in 2022 to about 2%, which suggests they are keeping cash to invest.
Data center builders lean more heavily on debt and have cut payouts, and the analysis leaves out off-balance-sheet commitments like leases, which may be large.
deep_dive.market_angle: The strongest balance sheets are at the big hyperscalers, which supports large-cap tech and the Nasdaq. The more debt-heavy builders such as the cloud names that leaned on Nvidia's financing carry more risk, so if AI spending slows they would be hit first, which could widen credit spreads for them.
deep_dive.trade_idea: A desk might buy VIX call spreads or Nasdaq put spreads as a hedge against a reversal in the AI rally, because volatility is cheaper after the 25.83% drop. The main risk is that the rally keeps going and the hedge decays to nothing.
note: Hyperscaler debt/assets fell from nearly 30% to about 25%, others near 34%.
Builders use more debt, chip firms use more cash.
Interview line: the AI boom is mostly funded by profits, but the debt-funded builders are the weak link.

deep_dive.why_now: Oil keeps inflation partly supply-driven while the Fed talks about higher rates, so how much a Fed move reaches long-term yields matters for the 10-year at 4.92%.
key_points: The San Francisco Fed finds the Fed responds more aggressively to demand-driven inflation than to supply-driven inflation.
Policy surprises pass mostly into longer-horizon forward rates when inflation is demand-driven.
Supply-side inflation pressures have grown since the pandemic, so Fed surprises are likely to have a smaller effect on longer-term yields.
The paper separates supply from demand by checking whether prices and quantities move in the same direction or opposite directions.
deep_dive.market_angle: If inflation stays supply-driven, hawkish Fed talk should push the 2-year yield up more than the 10-year, which flattens the yield curve from +29 basis points. The dollar could still gain on the short-end move.
deep_dive.trade_idea: A desk might consider a 2s10s flattener, betting the 2-year yield rises more than the 10-year if the Fed turns hawkish. The main risk is that oil-driven inflation fears push long-term yields up faster, which would steepen the curve instead.
note: Supply-driven inflation passes less into long yields.
Curve (10Y minus 2Y) is +29 bp now.
Interview line: when inflation comes from supply, Fed moves hit the front of the curve more than the back.

terms.def: A market bet that AI-linked companies will keep growing, like many people all crowding onto one side of a boat so it tips whenever they shift.
A gauge of expected stock swings that works like a fear meter, so it rises when investors are nervous and falls when they relax.
The line of interest rates from short loans to long loans to the government, like a price list that shows what lenders ask for different time frames.
Price increases that come from shortages or higher costs, like a storm that wipes out a crop, and rate hikes can't fix those the way they cool overheated demand.
A sign that an asset has risen so fast that it may need a rest, like a runner who sprinted too early and has to slow down.
Assets pledged to secure a loan, just like a car title you hand over when you borrow against your car.

cross_asset_notes: S&P 500 +4.73% to 7237.17 and Nasdaq +6.51% show how concentrated the market is in AI, so one name drove the whole day.
VIX -25.83% to 26.62 means fear eased a lot but is still well above a calm level, so the market is not fully relaxed.
10Y yield 4.92% (+1 bp) and 2Y 4.63% versus the Fed's 3.875% show hikes are partly priced, so Fed talk matters more than stocks for rates.
WTI -4.29% to 80.38 and gold +3.44% to 3636.3: cheaper oil eases inflation pressure, and the gold jump has no clear explanation.
take: The VIX fell 25.83% to 26.62 after Nvidia brought Huang back, but Congress is pushing back, there is a reported SEC probe and the Fed meets Dec 8 and 9. Would you buy or sell volatility here, and what single development would prove your call wrong?

10-year yield.def: The interest rate the US government pays to borrow money for 10 years. It also helps set the rates on things like mortgages and business loans.
10-year yield.analogy: It's like the interest rate on a 10-year loan that you make to the government.
10-year yield.today: It rose 1 basis point to 4.92%, a tiny move, because the worry-driven buying of safe Treasuries faded as stocks recovered.

AI trade.def: A market bet that companies tied to artificial intelligence will keep growing fast, so investors pile into the same group of stocks.
AI trade.analogy: It's like a crowd all standing on one side of a boat, so the boat tips whenever they shift.
AI trade.today: Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia revived the AI trade after the S&P 500 had fallen four straight weeks.

DLT.def: Short for distributed ledger technology, a shared digital record book that many computers keep in sync, which is the idea behind blockchains and tokenised assets.
DLT.analogy: It's like a shared online spreadsheet that everyone can see and no single person controls.
DLT.today: The ECB said it will accept assets issued on licensed DLT platforms as collateral, with details due in spring 2027 and the change planned for June 2027.

Nasdaq.def: A stock index that tracks a large group of companies, with a heavy weighting toward technology firms.
Nasdaq.analogy: It's like a report card for the tech classroom, so it swings more when tech has a big day.
Nasdaq.today: The Nasdaq rose 6.51% to 24089.56, beating the Dow because it holds so many AI-linked companies.

S&P 500.def: A stock index that follows 500 of the largest US companies and is the most common way to judge how the US stock market is doing.
S&P 500.analogy: It's like the overall grade for the whole school, but the biggest students count the most.
S&P 500.today: It rose 4.73% to 7237.17, its best day in more than a year, after four straight weekly declines.

Treasuries.def: Bonds sold by the US government to borrow money. Investors treat them as one of the safest places to park cash.
Treasuries.analogy: They're like IOUs from the government that people buy when they want to feel safe.
Treasuries.today: Last week worried investors bought Treasuries as a hiding place, and today that demand cooled as stocks rebounded.

VIX.def: A gauge of how much the market expects stocks to swing over the next month. It rises when investors are nervous and falls when they relax.
VIX.analogy: It's like a fear meter, or a weather forecast for how stormy stocks will be.
VIX.today: It dropped 25.83% to 26.62, which means fear eased a lot, but that level is still fairly nervous.

basis point.def: One hundredth of one percentage point, used to describe small changes in interest rates. So 100 basis points equals 1 percentage point.
basis point.analogy: It's like measuring a short walk in inches instead of miles.
basis point.today: The 10-year yield moved just 1 basis point, and the gap between the 10-year and 2-year yields is +29 basis points.

data center.def: A giant building full of computers and chips that stores data and runs AI programs and online services.
data center.analogy: It's like a huge power plant, except it produces computing power instead of electricity.
data center.today: A strategist warned that Wall Street is not pricing in a data center slowdown, which means a pullback in AI building could surprise investors.

dollar index.def: A number that tracks the US dollar against a basket of major currencies like the euro, yen and pound. When it rises, the dollar is getting stronger.
dollar index.analogy: It's like a scoreboard that shows how the dollar is doing against its main rivals.
dollar index.today: It rose 0.49% to 104.32, and headlines credit bets that the Fed will stay hawkish and not the midterm election.

overbought.def: A description of something that has risen so far and so fast that it may be due to slow down or pull back.
overbought.analogy: It's like a runner who sprinted the first mile and now needs to catch their breath.
overbought.today: Goldman's technical read says the dollar is overbought, so its next leg higher could slow even though the Fed outlook still supports it.

valuation.def: How expensive a stock or group of stocks is compared with the profits or sales the companies actually make.
valuation.analogy: It's like asking whether a house is priced fairly compared with what similar homes earn in rent.
valuation.today: Official papers have warned that AI valuations look stretched, which is part of why investors got so jumpy before today's bounce.

steps.label: Huang returns
steps.explain: Nvidia's board approved Jensen Huang's return as CEO after pressure from Trump.
steps.detail: Huang's exit on Nov 12 had kicked off a selloff in AI stocks. His return told investors that the leadership scare was over, at least for now.

steps.label: AI stocks jump
steps.explain: Shares of Nvidia and other AI-linked firms rose sharply because investors felt safer.
steps.detail: Nvidia helps finance the AI ecosystem, so firms like Oracle and CoreWeave also jumped on the bet that the money keeps flowing. That means the market was trading on confidence in one company.

steps.label: Nasdaq surges
steps.explain: The Nasdaq gained 6.51% because it holds so many AI-linked tech companies.
steps.detail: The S&P 500 rose 4.73% and the Dow rose 3.01%, so the broader market rose too, but less than tech. This was the best day for US stocks in more than a year.

steps.label: Fear drops
steps.explain: The VIX, the market's fear gauge, fell 25.83% to 26.62.
steps.detail: When stocks stop falling, investors pay less for protection against swings, so the VIX drops. At 26.62 it is still fairly nervous, and Congress and a reported SEC probe could bring the worry back.

steps.label: Gulf oil keeps flowing
steps.explain: Crude kept leaving the Persian Gulf even though attacks on tankers continue.
steps.detail: Traders had feared that attacks would choke off supply. Since barrels kept arriving, the supply fear faded, at least for today.

steps.label: WTI falls
steps.explain: WTI crude fell 4.29% to 80.38, its lowest settle since August.
steps.detail: Less supply fear means buyers are willing to pay less for oil. The price is still well above where it was before the Iran war, so this is a pullback and not a collapse.

steps.label: Inflation pressure eases
steps.explain: Cheaper oil lowers fuel and shipping costs, which feed into prices everywhere.
steps.detail: Gas prices matter to households, and shipping costs matter to businesses that pass them along. If oil stays lower, headline inflation has room to cool.

steps.label: Less pressure to hike
steps.explain: Central banks may feel a bit less pressure to raise interest rates.
steps.detail: The Fed's Williams still says higher rates are likely over time, so this is a small easing and not a change in direction. Cook warned that damaged infrastructure and low inventories could keep oil prices high for a long time, so the relief could fade.

steps.label: Williams signals hikes
steps.explain: Fed official John Williams said higher rates are likely over time to deal with inflation.
steps.detail: He also said he is confident inflation gets closer to 2% in 2027. Even so, the message that rates are heading up is what traders focused on.

steps.label: Hike bets build
steps.explain: Traders expect the Fed to raise rates, so short-term yields stay high.
steps.detail: The 2-year yield is 4.63% while the Fed's rate is 3.875%, so some hikes are already priced in. The 10-year barely moved, up 1 basis point to 4.92%, which fits the idea that oil-driven inflation passes less into long-term yields.

steps.label: Dollars look better
steps.explain: Higher US rates mean investors earn more by holding dollars than other currencies.
steps.detail: The Bank of Japan's 1.25% rate is 2.625 percentage points below the Fed's, and the ECB's 2.5% is also far below. So money is pulled toward dollar assets.

steps.label: Dollar index rises
steps.detail: Sterling and the euro edged up in the morning as the stock rebound trimmed the dollar's appeal, but the dollar was higher again by the close. Goldman's technical read says the dollar is overbought, so the next leg higher could slow.

quiz.q: The Nasdaq rose 6.51% while the Dow rose 3.01% after Huang's return. What best explains the gap?
options: The Dow holds more energy firms, which fell as crude lost 4.29%
The Nasdaq holds more AI-linked tech, which reacted most to Huang's return
The Dow holds more tech firms, which reacted most to Huang's return
The Nasdaq holds more food makers, which gained as oil got cheaper
quiz.explain: The Nasdaq is packed with AI-linked tech, so the Nvidia news hit it hardest. The Dow has much less of that exposure, so it rose by less.

quiz.q: Last week AI worries pulled Treasury yields lower. Why did the 10-year edge up 1 bp to 4.92% today?
options: Oil's drop to 80.38 stirred up fresh inflation worries for bond buyers
Fear-driven buying of safe Treasuries faded as stocks bounced back
Japan sold Treasuries to raise dollars for buying yen in the market
Williams announced a rate hike for the Dec 8 and 9 meeting
quiz.explain: Worried investors had bought safe Treasuries last week, which pushed yields down. When stocks recovered that safe-haven demand cooled, so yields stopped falling.

quiz.q: The VIX fell 25.83% to 26.62, so the debrief calls the market fully calm again.
options: True
False
quiz.explain: The VIX fell a lot, but 26.62 is still a fairly nervous level. Fear eased without disappearing.

quiz.q: The 10-year yield is 4.92% and the 2-year is 4.63%, a +29 bp gap. If inflation stays supply-driven and hawkish Fed talk lifts the 2-year more than the 10-year, what happens to that gap?
options: Up
Down
quiz.explain: Supply-driven inflation passes less into long-term yields, so the 2-year would catch up to the 10-year. That narrows the gap, which is called flattening, even though both yields might rise.

quiz.q: Kroger and Tyson were among the S&P 500's biggest losers as money chased growth. If the AI rally stalls on Nvidia scrutiny, what would these safer stocks probably do?
options: Up
Down
quiz.explain: They had been a hiding place amid cracks in the AI trade, so they sold off when the mood flipped. If the rally stalls, investors would likely drift back into them.

quiz.q: Goldman's technical read says the dollar index at 104.32 is overbought. If traders suddenly doubt the Fed will keep leaning hawkish, what would the dollar index probably do?
options: Up
Down
quiz.explain: Headlines credit the rally to hawkish Fed bets, not the election. If those bets cool, the extra yield from holding dollars shrinks, and an overbought dollar can fall quickly.

quiz.q: Put today's AI chain in order, from cause to effect.
items: Nvidia's board approves Huang's return after Trump's pressure
AI-linked stocks like Nvidia and Oracle jump
quiz.explain: The CEO news restored confidence, which lifted AI stocks, which lifted the indexes. Lower fear then showed up in the VIX.

quiz.q: Put the Fed-to-dollar chain in order, from cause to effect.
items: Williams says higher rates are likely over time
Markets price some hikes, with the 2-year at 4.63%
Dollars look more attractive to hold
quiz.explain: The hawkish message raised hike expectations, which made dollar assets pay more than other currencies. That pulled money into the dollar and lifted the index.

quiz.q: Headlines credit the dollar index's 0.49% rise to the Democratic midterm rout.
options: True
False
quiz.explain: Headlines credit hawkish Fed bets, not the election. The midterms started the dollar story, but today's move came from rate expectations.

quiz.q: The St. Louis Fed found hyperscalers' debt relative to assets fell to roughly 25% by early 2026, below other US firms near 34%.
options: True
False
quiz.explain: The ratio fell from nearly 30% in 2023 to roughly 25%, while other firms stayed near 34%. So the AI buildout is mostly funded by profits and not by extra borrowing.

quiz.q: How should a trader read Lagarde's 'Acting in time' speech, her last at the Frankfurt banking congress?
options: She said the ECB will cut rates to cushion Europe from energy costs
She told banks the ECB will hike its 2.5% rate at the next meeting
She urged acting early on problems, with no hint of an imminent move
She argued Europe should wait for problems to be obvious before acting
quiz.explain: Her theme was acting before a problem is obvious, but nothing in the headlines says the ECB is about to move. It's a theme and not a rate signal.

quiz.q: The 2-year yield is 4.63% while the Fed's rate is 3.875%. What does that gap tell you?
options: The Fed has already lifted its rate up to 4.63%
Markets already expect the Fed to raise rates over time
Bond buyers think Williams' 2027 inflation view is wrong
Investors expect the Fed to cut rates before 2027
quiz.explain: The 2-year tracks expected Fed policy closely. Sitting well above the current rate means traders already price in some hikes.

quiz.q: A San Francisco Fed paper says Fed surprises pass less into long yields when inflation is supply-driven. Why does that matter now?
options: Stock gains of 4.73% mean longer yields will now fall sharply this week
Oil-driven inflation means hawkish talk may lift the 2-year more than the 10-year
The Fed can fix oil shortages by raising short-term rates more quickly
Falling oil at 80.38 means inflation is now purely demand-driven again
quiz.explain: Inflation is partly driven by oil supply, so hawkish Fed news should show up mostly in short yields. That could flatten the +29 bp curve.

quiz.q: The dollar index rose 0.49% but USD/JPY slipped 0.49% to 158.93. What does the debrief say about the yen's move?
options: Japan stepped in again with a record intervention today
The BOJ raised its 1.25% rate to match the Fed's move
Weak Japanese inflation data cut the dollar's appeal
The reason isn't clear, since the dollar was broadly stronger
quiz.explain: The yen gained a little even though the dollar was stronger against most currencies, and the headlines don't explain why. So the honest answer is that the cause is unclear.

quiz.q: Kroger and Tyson Foods were among the S&P 500's biggest losers as Nvidia surged. What does that suggest?
options: Rising 10-year yields made staples too costly for investors to hold
Money left hiding places and went back into growth stocks
Cheaper oil at 80.38 squeezed food companies' profit margins
Consumers cut spending as the Fed hinted at higher interest rates
quiz.explain: Consumer stocks had been a safe bet amid cracks in the AI trade. When AI confidence returned, investors sold them to buy growth, so the move shows how fast the mood flipped.

quiz.q: WTI fell 4.29% to 80.38, its lowest settle since August. What drove the drop, according to the debrief?
options: China becoming the top oil buyer cut worldwide demand for crude
Crude kept flowing out of the Persian Gulf despite tanker attacks
Tanker attacks stopped and Gulf shipping returned to normal
Trump's remark about a giant hoax calmed worried oil traders
quiz.explain: Attacks on shipping continue, but oil kept leaving the Gulf anyway, so supply fear faded and prices fell. The other options blame events that don't explain today's move.
